'''Pilgrim High School''' (also known as '''Pilgrim''', or '''PHS''') is a [[suburban]] [[high school]] in the [[Pilgrim Park, Rhode Island|Pilgrim Park]] neighborhood of [[Warwick, Rhode Island]]. It is a part of [[Warwick Public Schools (Rhode Island)|Warwick Public Schools]]. The school is single-storied and features multiple hallways for specific subjects. Multiple renovations occurred in the school, most recently in 2016, before the consolidation process began.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shalvey |first1=Annie |title=Pilgrim undergoing renovations ahead of Warwick school consolidation |url=https://www.wpri.com/news/education/pilgrim-undergoing-renovations-ahead-of-warwick-school-consolidation/1044415715 |website=WPRI |date=30 June 2016 |publisher=Nexstar Broadcasting, Inc. |accessdate=4 May 2019}}</ref> The school logo is the shape of an [[American Revolution]] soldier head formed by the words "Pilgrim High School Patriots", although the letter "P" in the official colors is used for most athletic teams.

It opened during the middle of the 1963 school year to address overcrowding at [[Warwick Veterans High School]], which taught almost four thousand students at the time of opening.<ref name="beacon">{{cite news |last1=Coates |first1=Jennifer |title=Pilgrim to step back through decades at golden anniversary |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-to-step-back-through-decades-at-golden-anniversary,78761? |accessdate=4 May 2019 |work=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |date=January 31, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130203053434/http://www.warwickonline.com/stories/Pilgrim-to-step-back-through-decades-at-golden-anniversary,78761 |archive-date=3 February 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> Nevertheless, the new establishment eventually became notorious for the double session schedule to alleviate its own excess capacity problem by the late 1960s. Today, Pilgrim has an enrollment of 1,400 students thanks to a consolidation effort by the school department, after years of declining student population.

Pilgrim was historically well-known for sports, most notably the [[baseball]] team as they won multiple state championships all through a [[Sports dynasty|dynastic]] period. Most of the school's championships were won throughout the 1970s. In 2010s, the school's athletics entered a renaissance. Although the baseball team's last championship was in 1990, the boys' [[basketball]], unified basketball, competition [[cheerleading]], [[field hockey]], [[American football|football]], [[gymnastics]] boys' [[ice hockey]], boys' and girls' [[lacrosse]], boys' and girls' [[soccer]], girls' indoor and outdoor track running, and unified [[volleyball]] teams won division championships in the 2010s and 2020s.<ref name="rihssports champs">{{cite web |last1=D'Angelo |first1=Tommy |title=RIIL Team State Championships |url=http://www.rihssports.com/CHAMPIONSHIPS%20ORGANIZED/BY%20SCHOOL/School%20Pages.html |website=Rhode Island High School Sports |publisher=RIHSSports.com |accessdate=4 May 2019 == History ==
=== Background and opening era (1960s) ===
In the early 1960s, the early [[Mid-twentieth century baby boom|baby boom]] population began entering high school, and the population of Warwick skyrocketed to almost 70,000 residents during the post-war era with the popularity of the suburb. To accommodate the sudden growth of families, in 1955, the city consolidated all of its then-operating high schools at the time into one building, [[Warwick Veterans High School]]. The former establishments, Aldrich, Gorton, and Lockwood, were converted into [[Middle school#United States|junior high schools]]. All of them have since closed, with Gorton becoming Warwick Public Schools' main offices in 2016, and Lockwood shuttering in June, 1979, now redeveloped into [[Condominium (living space)|condominium]]s.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bower |first1=Matt |title=New school feeder plan approved |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/new-school-feeder-plan-approved,106607? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=4 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160309212836/http://warwickonline.com/stories/new-school-feeder-plan-approved,106607 |archive-date=9 March 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Howell |first1=John |title=Gorton proposed for school offices |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/gorton-proposed-for-school-offices,107773? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=4 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160317000238/http://warwickonline.com/stories/gorton-proposed-for-school-offices,107773 |archive-date=17 March 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Howell |first1=John |title=City to seek proposals for use of Aldrich |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/city-to-seek-proposals-for-use-of-aldrich,119562 |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=4 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117223117/http://warwickonline.com/stories/city-to-seek-proposals-for-use-of-aldrich,119562 |archive-date=17 November 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Overcrowding was still a problem only years after Vets opened, despite serving only three grades. It experimented with staggered schedules for the tenth graders, leading towards a double session schedule shortly after.<ref name="mike">{{cite journal |last1=Morry |first1=Michael A. |title=Scheduling Two Schools In One Building |journal=NASSP Bulletin |date=March 1, 1964 |volume=48 |issue=290 |page=99 |doi=10.1177/019263656404829014 |s2cid=145737517 }}</ref> The overpopulated student body led to the construction of a new high school in the city. It is unknown how the school got its name, but it presumably originates from where the neighborhood the school is located, Pilgrim Park. On December 30, 1962, the school was officially dedicated, and Michael A. Morry was named the first principal. A month later, on January 29, the school opened without delay during a cold winter morning. The big move was efficiently managed, with the Vets secretary going as far as scheduling students in the same classes they had in their previous school. The courtyards full of landscaping were described by one student as "just beautiful", and the cafeteria (once known as the "dining hall") was used to hold delightful dances. Sports teams were already formed, and the gymnasium was prepared to hold its first [[basketball]] game.<ref name="beacon" />

Still, Pilgrim's student population kept increasing. Morry implemented the double session schedule to avoid cramped conditions at the new school.<ref>{{cite web |title=City has 8 to 10 too many schools |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/city-has-8-to-10-too-many-schools,102246 |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=4 May 2019 |quote=I remember when the Warwick High Schools had DOUBLE sessions and each high school had 3000 students. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160127190642/http://warwickonline.com/stories/city-has-8-to-10-too-many-schools,102246 |archive-date=27 January 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== The golden era (1970–early 90s) ===
Despite the population peaking in the early 1970s, the number of students attending Pilgrim contributed to athletics, and they are responsible for the success of sports teams throughout the decade{{Clarify|date=November 2021}}. In 1968, the boys' [[cross country running|cross country]] team gave the school its first division championship, ushering an era of Pilgrim's dominance in athletics. The following year, the cross country team gave Pilgrim its first state title.

The baseball team was still consistent when they first played in 1963, and in 1970, they won their first championship, the first of five in the decade. In the 1970s, Pilgrim's baseball team had a 110–34 record (a 76.4% win percentage), six division titles, and five state titles starting in 1970, a threepeat from 1972 to 1974, and 1978. Pilgrim lost the championship in 1979, but their power continued until 1984, when the team finished off with a losing record. Although the baseball team in the 1980s was inconsistent with their records, they managed to win the 1980 and 1990 championships. and competed for the 1992 title.<ref name="rihssports bb">{{cite web |last1=D'Angelo |first1=Tommy |title=Baseball Team W\L Records |url=http://www.rihssports.com/RECORDS/BOYS/Baseball%20Records.html |website=Rhode Island High School Sports |publisher=RIHSSports.com |accessdate=5 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190731121849/http://rihssports.com/RECORDS/BOYS/Baseball%20Records.html |archive-date=31 July 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Pilgrim also won championships with other sports teams as well. Boys' cross country continued to win titles through 1987. Ice hockey won three straight division championships from 1974 to 1976, and another in 1990. Football, [[wrestling]], [[field hockey]], boys' [[indoor track]], girls' soccer, girls' [[tennis]], and girls' [[volleyball]] were teams also associated with the "golden era".<ref name="rihss">{{cite web |last1=D'Angelo |first1=Tommy |title=School Team Championship Pages |url=http://www.rihssports.com/CHAMPIONSHIPS%20ORGANIZED/BY%20SCHOOL/School%20Pages.html |website=Rhode Island High School Sports |publisher=RIHSSports.com |accessdate=5 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190308010231/http://www.rihssports.com/CHAMPIONSHIPS%20ORGANIZED/BY%20SCHOOL/School%20Pages.html |archive-date=8 March 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The famed Morry had the Pilgrim football field dedicated to him. After he retired in 1983, Morry was succeeded by incumbent vice principal Ralph J. Hoffman. However, the latter was named as the school department's [[hearing officer]], and in 1987, he left the school.<ref>{{cite web |title=RALPH J. HOFFMAN |url=http://cranstononline.com/stories/ralph-j-hoffman,41745 |website=Cranston Herald |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=5 May 2019}}</ref> Edmund B. "Smiley"Miley served as the principal of Pilgrim after Hoffman, a tenure that would last until 2002. He was derisively nicknamed "Smiley" by students due to his serious demeanor.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

=== Post-golden era (early 90s–2014) ===
After years of instability, some teams began to emerge from an era where they lacked championships. The baseball team continued to appear in the playoffs, while the girls' cross country team won their first division title. The football team made two appearances in the division championship in 1992 and 1995. Boys' soccer, boys' [[Swimming (sport)|swimming]], girls' basketball, girls' cross country, girls' indoor track, softball, and wrestling are some of the notable teams that won titles in the 1990s to the early 2000s. The school's second track was installed in 1995 to replace the original cinder track, and was used frequently that it showed decrepit conditions twenty years later.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dolan |first1=Kelcy |title=19 years later, Pilgrim track full of pot holes |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/19-years-later-pilgrim-track-full-of-pot-holes,94382? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications}}</ref>

When Miley retired from office, Victor Mercurio (now superintendent of [[East Greenwich, Rhode Island|East Greenwich]] schools) took over duties of overseeing the students of Pilgrim, until he was appointed as the school department's director of secondary education in 2004.<ref>{{cite web |title=PILGRIM FACULTY & STAFF 2000 - 2001 |url=http://www.pilgrimhs.org/Home_Page/Faculty_staff.htm |website=Pilgrim High School |publisher=Warwick Public Schools |accessdate=5 May 2019 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20030808053315/http://pilgrimhs.org/Home%20Page/Faculty_staff.htm |archivedate=August 8, 2003 |date=October 29, 2002}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Victor Mercurio, Ed.D. - Superintendent - East Greenwich School Department |url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/victor-mercurio-ed-d |website=LinkedIn |publisher=LinkedIn Corporation |accessdate=5 May 2019}}</ref> Dennis Mullen became the first teacher in the school named principal at Pilgrim, and he won the Outstanding New Principal award by the Rhode Island Association of School Principals. He also earned Principal of the Year in 2010 by the same organization. His tenure ended in 2012 similarly to his predecessor, taking over the job as director of secondary education.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Howell |first1=John |title='Too much testing,' says Mullen as he bows out of Warwick schools |url=http://cranstononline.com/stories/toomuchtestingsaysmullenashebowsoutofwarwickschools,104399 |website=Cranston Herald |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=5 May 2019}}</ref> Marie Cote (née Johnson) became the school's first female principal, a position she would hold until 2015.<ref>{{cite web |title=Administration |url=http://www.pilgrimhs.org/Departments_Administration.html |website=Pilgrim High School |publisher=Warwick Public Schools |accessdate=5 May 2019 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130403042100/http://www.pilgrimhs.org/Departments_Administration.html |archivedate=April 3, 2013}}</ref>

One notable lowlight during Pilgrim's post-golden era included a traffic accident during the 2009 school year. In April that year, fifteen-year old sophomore Kimberly Pisaturo was crossing the street while wearing headphones and looking at her phone, when a school bus transporting students to Providence struck her near the school. The driver, Rebecca Toolin, was unaware of the situation until she pulled over. The victim's family requested privacy due to the tragedy, but a YouTube video was uploaded in memory of her.<ref>{{cite web |agency=NBC 10 News |title=Police ID student killed by school bus |url=https://turnto10.com/archive/police-id-student-killed-by-school-bus |website=Turn to 10 |publisher=Sinclair Broadcast Group |accessdate=5 May 2019 |date=May 1, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=EKUN957 |title=IN LOVING MEMORY OF A PILGRIM HIGH SCHOOL STUDENT KILLED BY A SCHOOL BUS IN WARWICK, RHODE ISLAND |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gV9sSz3f3T8 |url-status=dead |website=YouTube |publisher=Google, Inc. |date=May 8, 2009 |access-date=May 5, 2019 |archive-date=March 20, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230320204742/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gV9sSz3f3T8&gl=US&hl=en }}</ref>

Students' disinterest in metalwork helped convert one room from a shop classroom and storage area to a media studio for [[audiovisual]] courses as a result of a $95,600 grant by The Champlin Foundations late in 2013. The plan was conceived the previous year when the faculty created a movie and screened it as a fundraising event by the Pilgrim Film Society club. Principal Cote, along with two English teachers, a music teacher, and a technology education teacher, were involved with filling out the application required to acquire the grant. With the money, the budget allowed eight [[iMac]] desktops with preloaded applications for appropriate classes, audio and camera equipment, lighting fixtures, microphones, and the like.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rodrigues |first1=Jennifer |title=Coming to Pilgrim: High-tech Studio 107 |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/coming-to-pilgrim-high-tech-studio-107,88408? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications}}</ref>

==== 1989 acid incident ====
Around that time, drug use was rampant in the lavatories, that an incident involving numerous students occurred on April 6, 1989. The preceding evening, a student, identified as "[[John Doe|Student Doe]]", met with Student A and talked about purchasing [[LSD]]. The conversation occurred at Student B's house, though the latter had no knowledge such conversation occurred, but knew Student A was going to get drugs. The next morning, Doe entered the building thirty minutes after the first bell. It was said that Doe visited the lavatory every time before classes, and has no idea why he does so. Meanwhile, Student B witnessed Student A accompanying another student. All three were spooked by a teacher approaching. The student with Student A entered first prior to Doe, and took out a [[cigarette]]. Doe went inside the bathroom after, before Students A and B entered. When two other unnamed individuals went inside, the trade commenced. It took approximately five to ten minutes to complete the deal, but out of nowhere, Principal Miley was conducting searches for students hiding in lavatories, and happened to find everyone loitering inside. They were all told to report to the office immediately. After denying that a transaction occurred in the lavatory, Doe received a suspension for tardiness.

Soon after, the student walked to a nearby [[Mister Donut]]. One of the students that were with him in the lavatory offered him some acid. The group of students involved then moved on to the [[McDonald's]] located in the former Warwick Plaza (now a [[Walmart]]), where Doe obtained thirty hits of acid after following instructions of a student that purchased the drug from another person (Student A) that was part of the group in the lavatory. Doe hid the acid in his cigarette pack. Later that day, Doe returned to "B"'s house, where they found out from a classmate that "somebody flipped out at school", and "A"'s father was attempting to find the students involved or his own son. As the father knew "B" was included as part of the group, Doe fled out of the house in fear of uncertain harm.

After an investigation that found several students feeling sick from using drugs that day, Miley recommended the suspension to be extended until April 6, 1990, though the principal had no personal knowledge of Doe's involvement in the drug trade. He stated that it was the first time the student was disciplined for violating school policy on the sale, use, and/or possession of drugs. The incident was reviewed by the [[Rhode Island Department of Elementary and Secondary Education|Rhode Island Department of Education]] as ''John M. Doe v. Warwick School Committee''. The findings concluded that a drug transaction did occur in the lavatory, and that Doe lied about not witnessing it. The student was not found as a participant in a [[Conspiracy (criminal)|conspiracy]] to sell LSD that day, and was not responsible for Student A's distribution of drugs. On November 8, 1989, the case was decided to have the school [[Expungement|expunge]] Student Doe's disciplinary records relating to the suspension, and to let him return to class.<ref>{{cite web |title=John M. Doe v. Warwick School Committee |url=http://www2.ride.ri.gov/applications/RideDirectory/DOCS/1989/0035-89-John_M_Doe_v_Warwick_110889.pdf |website=RIDE |publisher=Rhode Island Department of Elementary and Secondary Education |accessdate=5 May 2019 |date=November 8, 1989 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161229072527/http://www2.ride.ri.gov/applications/RideDirectory/DOCS/1989/0035-89-John_M_Doe_v_Warwick_110889.pdf |archive-date=29 December 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Consolidation era and sports renaissance (2011–present) ===
In late 2011, talks about consolidating Warwick's secondary schools surfaced. The committee reviewed options for the fates of the affected schools, and what strategies the department would apply to benefit unifying them. Some alternatives included closing two junior highs and sending all students to an old senior high, converting to a 7–12 model, or closing only one school.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bower |first1=Matt |title=Panel considers closing 2 jr. highs |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/panel-considers-closing-2-jr-highs,65213? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |accessdate=5 May 2019}}</ref> The school department already once considered 7–12 schools in the early 1980s according to a report by local television station [[WJAR]], but faded into insignificance as times passed.{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}} The plans were put on hold<ref>{{cite web |last1=Howell |first1=John |title=Plan to close school on hold for now |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/plan-to-close-school-on-hold-for-now,67446? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications}}</ref> until 2013, when the department's Long Term Facilities Planning Committee developed scenarios for a five-year plan on the futures of the secondary schools. Pilgrim's student population was one-third than it had in the late 1960s, as 1,021 were attending during the 2014 school year.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rodrigues |first1=Jennifer |title=Panel calls for consolidation of schools |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/panel-calls-for-consolidation-of-schools,84637? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications}}</ref>

The following year, the school committee decided to close Aldrich and Gorton junior high schools and convert Vets into one middle school by the 2017 school year, officially known as "Alternative 5". The 7–12 plan for Pilgrim and Vets returned as well, but it was voted off prior the decision. The Long Term Facilities Planning Committee hired an independent consultant, Symmes Maini & McKee Associates, to study the entire district and develop plans, for $238,243.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bower |first1=Matt |title=Aldrich, Gorton to close, but no timetable set |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/aldrich-gorton-to-close-but-no-timetable-set,103192? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721090536/http://www.warwickonline.com/stories/Aldrich-Gorton-to-close-but-no-timetable-set,103192 |archive-date=2015-07-21 |url-status=live }}</ref> In October, the new feeder plan was established, where ten elementary schools are to attend the new Vets Middle School, and Pilgrim when the students reach ninth grade. Throughout the 2016 school year, Vets students and parents were given an inside look of what Pilgrim would resemble after the consolidation. Then-Vets principal Gerald Habershaw presented a PowerPoint for concerned parents, and was named principal once the two schools merged, replacing interim principal Pamela Bernardi.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bower |first1=Matt |title=Vets students, parents learn what to expect with move to Pilgrim |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/vets-students-parents-learn-what-to-expect-with-move-to-pilgrim,109433? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170705225535/http://www.warwickonline.com/stories/vets-students-parents-learn-what-to-expect-with-move-to-pilgrim,109433 |archive-date=2017-07-05 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On the first day of the "new" Pilgrim, traffic stopped in the middle of Warwick Avenue, and the street leading towards drop-off roads and back parking lots were congested and unorganized. Vets students found themselves unable to find their buses, and even police officers attempted to guide motorists, but with no success. Habershaw described the [[traffic jam]] as a "perfect storm". Some parents found alternate routes by dropping their children off at the nearby Holliman Elementary, which prompted administrators to consider opening a drop-off route there, but no developments occurred.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Howell |first1=John |title=Pilgrim exodus brings traffic to standstill |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-exodus-brings-traffic-to-standstill,115918? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111205602/http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-exodus-brings-traffic-to-standstill,115918 |archive-date=2016-11-11 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Today, the students of Pilgrim experienced what many consider a renaissance. The establishment of more clubs occurred as the teachers' union successfully negotiated a contract effective November 2017.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=John |title=Warwick teachers OK contracts by 'wide margin,' ending 2-year labor dispute |url=https://www.providencejournal.com/news/20171122/warwick-teachers-ok-contracts-by-wide-margin-ending-2-year-labor-dispute |website=Providence Journal |publisher=GateHouse Media, LLC}}</ref> A political involvement club, established by a 2019 graduate of the school and an English teacher, attracts diverse numbers of students on learning debates, gaining confidence, and meeting actual politicians to help keep the club running and discuss certain topics involving the government.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hartley |first1=Ethan |title=Pilgrim class president starts politics club |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-class-president-starts-politics-club,130042? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171211202356/http://www.warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-class-president-starts-politics-club,130042 |archive-date=2017-12-11 |url-status=live }}</ref> However, the club saw no activity after 2018.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

The baseball team continues to finish off most seasons with winning records, but not close to the potent 1970s teams.<ref name="rihssports bb" /> The football team, with the support of new coaching staff and a 4–3 record, reached the playoffs to compete in a rematch against [[Central Falls High School|Central Falls]] for the division title in 2018, but only to lose 14–10 at the conclusion of the game.<ref name="rihssports fb" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Central Falls vs Pilgrim|url=https://www.maxpreps.com/games/football-fall-18/central-falls-vs-pilgrim/11-17-2018-iNXObqnKq0OX0JPB42zdUQ.htm#tab=box-score&schoolid=|website=MaxPreps|publisher=CBS Interactive}}</ref> [[Cheerleading]], [[field hockey]], [[Special Olympics#Unified Sports|unified]] basketball, boys' basketball, boys' ice hockey, boys' soccer, girls' ice hockey, girls' [[lacrosse]], girls' soccer, girls' indoor and [[outdoor track]] teams were known for winning titles during the sports revival era.<ref name="rihssports champs" />

==== Homecoming Dance Controversy ====
On November 6, 2021, a time when [[COVID-19]] cases were rising in the state, a video surfaced on the internet showing principal Gerald Habershaw without a mask alongside students at Pilgrim's annual homecoming dance.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-11-16|title=Pilgrim High Officials: RIDOH Believes Covid Outbreak is Connected to School Dance|url=https://www.abc6.com/video-shows-maskless-principal-students-before-covid-19-outbreak/|access-date=2021-11-28|website=ABC6|language=en-US}}</ref> Soon after, Pilgrim saw a rise in COVID-19 cases, reporting 59 new student cases and 6 new faculty cases soon after the homecoming dance. As a result, the school moved to distance learning, which ended on November 29.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Reynolds|first=Mark|title=Pilgrim High School principal's job status uncertain after unmasked homecoming dance|url=https://www.providencejournal.com/story/news/education/2021/11/27/pilgrim-high-school-principals-fate-uncertain-after-caught-unmasked/8766703002/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=The Providence Journal|language=en-US}}</ref>

On November 22, Habershaw was placed on paid leave until further investigation, with assistant principal Pam Bernardi becoming acting principal until further notice. However, on November 27, Habershaw unexpectedly died from a heart attack at the age of 57.<ref>{{Cite web|last=NEWS|first=SAMANTHA LATOS, NBC 10|date=2021-11-27|title=Pilgrim High School Principal Gerald Habershaw dies of heart attack|url=https://turnto10.com/news/local/pilgrim-high-school-principal-gerald-habershaw-dies-of-heart-attack|access-date=2021-12-17|website=WJAR}}</ref> Later that day, his brother revealed that Habershaw tested positive for COVID-19 a few days after the homecoming dance but was recovering. Habershaw had been fully vaccinated and was not hospitalized leading up to his death.<ref>{{Cite web|first1=Antonia Noori|last1=Farzan|authorlink1=Antonia Noori Farzan|first2=Tom|last2=Mooney|title=Pilgrim High School principal Habershaw died of COVID complications, says his brother|url=https://www.providencejournal.com/story/news/local/2021/11/27/warwick-pilgrim-high-school-principal-gerald-habershaw-dies/8783018002/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=The Providence Journal|language=en-US}}</ref>

On November 28, a memorial service was held at the high school, with hundreds attending.<ref>{{Cite web|last=NEWS|first=CAL DYMOWSKI, NBC 10|date=2021-11-28|title=Pilgrim High School community gathers for candle vigil in honor of Gerry Habershaw|url=https://turnto10.com/news/local/pilgrim-high-school-community-gathers-for-candle-vigil-in-honor-of-gerry-habershaw|access-date=2021-11-29|website=WJAR}}</ref>

=== 2022 Election Demolition and Replacement Ballot Measure ===
During the 2022 Midterm Elections, the City of Warwick introduced a local ballot measure that would have the city put aside $350 Million in bonds to demolish Pilgrim and Toll Gate High School and replace them with newer, more modern high school buildings. The ballot measure passed by a margin of 58.8% to 41.2%<ref>{{Cite web |title=RI.gov: Election Results |url=https://www.ri.gov/election/results/2022/general_election/races/503.html |access-date=2022-11-13 |website=www.ri.gov}}</ref>

=== Activities and events ===
Throughout the year, Pilgrim hosts events to attract students, alumni, and residents alike. Most of the proceeds go to funding various after-school events and clubs. Fundraisers are periodically held to raise money for the clubs and senior projects.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kalunian |first1=Karen |title=Pilgrim senior project to benefit kids seeking homes |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-senior-project-to-benefit-kids-seeking-homes-families,133120? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180416110835/http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-senior-project-to-benefit-kids-seeking-homes-families,133120 |archive-date=2018-04-16 |url-status=live }}</ref> Both the junior and senior [[prom]]s are held, always one week apart from each other. The senior After-Prom Extravaganza (commonly referred to as APE) was first celebrated in 2008 after two graduates of Pilgrim died in an accident involving a drunk driver.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dolan |first1=Kelcy |title=Pilgrim principal, parents recruiting volunteers for post-prom extravaganza |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-principal-parents-recruiting-volunteers-for-post-prom-extravaganza,109099? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160529021900/http://www.warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-principal-parents-recruiting-volunteers-for-post-prom-extravaganza,109099 |archive-date=2016-05-29 |url-status=live }}</ref> Pilgrim Idol is the official musical [[talent show]] of the school, with contestants judged by staff members and local radio station DJs.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Howell |first1=John |title=The show must go on |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/sa-idol,130301? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171222061300/http://warwickonline.com/stories/sa-idol,130301 |archive-date=2017-12-22 |url-status=live }}</ref> Another talent show, locally known as the ''Follies'', is a showcase of comedic, musical, and other performing arts talent.<ref>{{cite web |title=Did you hear... |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/did-you-hear,34616? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications}}</ref> Near the beginning of the final exam week, seniors decorate the sidewalks with chalk. The tradition originated at Vets, but was quickly adopted by Pilgrim in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |title=An art break before finals |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/sa-art,134122? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications |access-date=2019-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180525062226/http://warwickonline.com/stories/sa-art,134122 |archive-date=2018-05-25 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Sports==
As a member of the [[Rhode Island Interscholastic League]], the Pilgrim Patriots was known in the 1970s for earning multiple division and state championships. By the end of the 1990s thru the 2010s, however, the Patriots suffered a period of time winning only a small number of championships. Since then, the Patriots found themselves successful again by the late 2010s. Athletic participation requires good academic standing. Students are taught that they represent the school as a whole while playing in sports.<ref name="phs sp">{{cite web |title=Athletics |url=https://phs.warwickschools.org/activities/athletics/ |website=Pilgrim High School |publisher=Warwick Public Schools}}</ref>

===Sports offered===
Pilgrim offers sixteen sports for their students to have an opportunity to play in:<ref name="phs sp" />
*[[Baseball]] (boys only)
*[[Basketball]]
*[[Cheerleading]]
*[[Cross country running|Cross country]]
*[[Field hockey]] (girls only)
*[[Golf]] (co-ed)
*[[Gymnastics]] (girls only, in cooperation with Toll Gate)
*[[High school football|Football]] (boys only)
*[[Ice hockey]]
*[[Lacrosse]]
*[[Soccer]]
*[[Softball]] (girls only)
*[[Swimming (sport)|Swimming]]
*[[Tennis]]
*[[Track and field]] (indoor and outdoor)
*[[Volleyball]]
*[[Wrestling]] (co-ed)

[[Special Olympics#Unified Sports|Unified]] basketball and volleyball are also offered, and its teams compete in the RIIL tournament. [[Rugby union]] is also offered, but it is not an official RIIL sport. Pilgrim is the first and so far the only public high school in the state to compete in rugby matches.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sponseller |first1=Alex |title=Pilgrim becomes first public school in RI to play rugby |url=http://warwickonline.com/stories/pilgrim-rugby,142008? |website=Warwick Beacon |publisher=Beacon Communications}}</ref>
